NASA warns this year's Monster El Niño could be even bigger than legendary 1997 event

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that NASA scientists are tracking an exceptionally powerful El Niño that could grow even larger than the historic 1997 event, which brought extreme weather to regions around the world.
  • El Niño is a recurring climate phenomenon that typically develops every two to seven years, when ocean temperatures rise above normal across parts of the equatorial Pacific.
  • Industry observers note that two of the most powerful recent El Niño events occurred in 1997-98 and 2015-16.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NASA scientists are tracking an exceptionally powerful El Niño that could grow even larger than the historic 1997 event, which brought extreme weather to regions around the world. Using 35 years of satellite observations, researchers can now compare the rapidly developing 2026 El Niño with some of the strongest events ever recorded, revealing remarkable similarities and important differences.

El Niño is a recurring climate phenomenon that typically develops every two to seven years, when ocean temperatures rise above normal across parts of the equatorial Pacific. These changes can disrupt atmospheric circulation and alter weather patterns far beyond the Pacific Ocean.

Industry observers note that two of the most powerful recent El Niño events occurred in 1997-98 and 2015-16. Both had widespread consequences, including destructive fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, severe drought and crop failures in southern Africa, and intense rainfall and coastal flooding in Southern California. Now, the 2026 El Niño is emerging as another major event, with satellite data suggesting it could rival those historic episodes.

How El Niño Builds Strength in the Pacific.

The development of El Niño depends on a complex interaction between ocean temperatures and atmospheric winds.

According to recent reports, under normal conditions, steady trade winds push warm surface water toward the western Pacific Ocean. This causes warm water to accumulate in the west, where the ocean surface sits slightly higher than it does farther east.

In a recent development, when the trade winds weaken, some of that warm water begins moving eastward across the Pacific. The shift can weaken the winds even further or occasionally cause them to reverse direction. This allows additional warm water to spread east, reinforcing the process and raising ocean temperatures and sea levels across the central and eastern Pacific.

Sources indicate that although the underlying process is similar each time, no two El Niño events develop in exactly the same way. Their behavior depends partly on where the warmest water accumulates and how the atmosphere responds to the changing ocean conditions.

"The search for the 'typical' El Niño is very elusive," stated Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). "They're all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.".

NASA Satellites Reveal Striking Similarities to 1997.

To understand how the current El Niño compares with earlier events, scientists are examining decades of satellite measurements of ocean surface height.

This technique, called satellite altimetry, measures subtle changes in the elevation of the ocean surface. Because seawater expands as it becomes warmer, unusually high sea levels in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific can reveal where heat is accumulating during El Niño.

In a recent development, NASA's comparison maps show differences in Pacific Ocean surface height on October 13, 1997 (left), and October 12, 2026 (right). The earlier measurements were collected by the TOPEX/Poseidon satellite, while the newer observations came from the Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich satellite. Scientists at JPL processed both datasets to make the events easier to compare.

According to recent reports, the maps use red to identify areas where the ocean surface is higher than its usual level, while white represents normal conditions and blue demonstrates areas where sea levels are below average. To better isolate the effects of El Niño and other temporary natural changes, researchers removed variations associated with seasonal patterns and long-term trends.

According to recent reports, one major advantage of these observations is their remarkable consistency. Successive satellite missions have followed nearly identical paths, with overlapping periods of operation that allow scientists to compare measurements across decades.

"What's unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next," Willis stated. "That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.".

Why the 2026 El Niño Resembles a Historic Climate Giant.

Recent findings suggest that the 2026 El Niño intensified much more abruptly than the powerful 1997-98 event. Despite that difference in timing, NASA's satellite measurements from October reveal striking similarities in how the two events are developing.

In both cases, the Pacific displays a pronounced difference in sea level (low in the west and high in the east). The observations also show elevated, unusually warm water stretching eastward along the equator until it reaches the coast of South America.

Recent findings suggest that these similarities suggest that the 2026 event could produce weather effects resembling those experienced during the 1997-98 El Niño. That earlier episode brought substantial rainfall to California and other parts of the southern United States, raising the possibility of comparable conditions during the coming winter.

However, the powerful 2015-16 El Niño demonstrates why similarities in overall strength do not necessarily translate into identical weather impacts.

In a recent development, for that comparison, NASA scientists also examined ocean surface height measurements from October 12, 2015, recorded by the Jason-2 satellite. The data were placed alongside observations from approximately the same time of year in 1997 and 2026.

Although the 2015 event also featured exceptionally warm water and elevated sea levels along the equator, that warm water did not extend toward the South American coast as strongly as it did during the other two events.

In a recent development, the resulting rainfall patterns were different as well. During the winter of 2015-16, much of the precipitation associated with El Niño was concentrated over Central America and the southeastern United States, while Mexico experienced significant flooding.

Will El Niño Bring Extreme Weather in Winter 2026-27?

The latest observations have prompted scientists to closely monitor how the 2026 El Niño develops and what it could mean for weather conditions in the months ahead.

In its October 8, 2026, outlook, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) estimated an 83 percent chance that strong to very strong El Niño conditions would occur during the first three months of 2027.

That forecast points to the potential for a particularly significant climate event, but it does not establish exactly where the most severe effects will occur.

El Niño can influence weather across much of the planet by changing the movement of heat and moisture through the atmosphere. However, those effects become increasingly difficult to predict farther from the tropical Pacific, where other atmospheric processes can alter or weaken the expected patterns.

As a result, even the strong resemblance between the 2026 and 1997 events cannot guarantee that the coming winter will unfold in the same way.

"There's always a bit of a dice roll here," Willis said. "Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn't mean it will be exactly the same -- it's just our best guess at the moment.".

The unprecedented consistency of the satellite record gives researchers a valuable way to recognize familiar patterns and evaluate the scale of the developing El Niño. But whether 2026-27 ultimately matches the extreme weather of previous historic events will depend on how the ocean and atmosphere interact in the months ahead.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In their (slightly belated) upcoming years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

In a recent development, this, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Industry observers note that understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s upcoming ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”.

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of newly introduced Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post states that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Sources indicate that future releases, of course, include fresh The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.).

It has been revealed that the qualifier left no room for error. It was a single-elimination bracket for 256 teams, and every match was a best-of-three. Once reinstated, Aurora did not drop a map before the final. They beat Pixel Lumina 2-0 in the second semi-final.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for enthusiasts, tire shopping is an upgrade, not a chore. While the casual driver might treat new tires like regular maintenance, anyone who cares about vehicle dynamics knows that what meets the road defines how a truck or SUV rides, tracks, and stops. It is the single most transformative upgrade you can make to your vehicle. For more than 110 years, Cooper tires have catered to drivers who look past the showroom floor and seek out products that overdeliver on performance, capability, and long-term durability.

According to recent reports, and that level of purpose-built engineering is more vital than ever. As vehicles grow heavier and more capable, tires need to do more than simply roll down an interstate. They have to withstand heavy payload demands, sudden weather changes, and unpredictable pavement. Cooper tires are built to that benchmark. Rooted in American engineering and real-world development, Cooper tires are built to an uncompromising standard that live up to their promises. From the rock-crawling STT Pro to the severe-snow-designated Stronghold AT, the Discoverer® family has earned its reputation through real-world testing from Alaskan ice to jagged mountain trails.

The latest Cooper Discoverer® HT adapts that rugged all-terrain lineage for long-distance highway cruising, matching heavy-duty capability with quiet, refined composure. While it retains the structural durability to wander down a gravel trail with a trailer in tow, its core mission is maximizing comfort and control across hundreds of miles of open road.

Recent findings suggest that where many highway tires trade load capability for a soft ride, the Discoverer® HT is engineered to handle both. Straight, reinforced sidewalls provide the structural foundation needed to maintain an optimal contact patch under load. Whether the vehicle is running light or carrying family, gear, and tongue weight, the tire resists deformation, ensuring consistent steering response and predictable roadholding grip in any condition. It’s engineered for drivers whose tires have to hold their own—providing a dependable, hard-working partner that won’t fold when the truck or SUV is pushed to its limit.

Cooper tires also tackle truck and SUV tire performance, with advanced features. Its proprietary 3-D Micro-Gauge Siping incorporates interlocking zig-zag sipes inside the tread blocks. Under heavy braking, sharp turns, or loaded acceleration, these interlocking sipes lock together to stiffen the tread block, to help support responsiveness. Crucially, these sipes run deep into the tread rubber, ensuring that gripping edges are still present to help with traction. That structural integrity backs up an exceptional UTQG treadwear rating of 720 and a 70,000-mile limited treadwear warranty on passenger fitments.

According to recent reports, this is the tire for drivers who expect their trucks or suvs to show up for the long haul. Whether that means towing a camper into the backcountry, handling moving-day payloads, or eating up cross-country interstate miles in quiet comfort, the mission remains the same: a single set of tires that balances real-world traction, refined manners, and hard-working capability.

To fit that wide spectrum of work, Cooper offers the Discoverer® HT across 19 passenger sizes covering 16- to 22-inch wheels (with section widths from 245 to 285 mm), alongside 16 light-truck (LT) options engineered with deeper tread grooves and higher load ratings. Backed by a 45-day satisfaction guarantee and over a century of research and development, the Discoverer® HT delivers what Cooper has always stood for: the quiet confidence that the job was done right.

#52028. Latest Update: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1267 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful.
  • Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain.
  • Sources indicate that the finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an notable opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

Sources indicate that the finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

Sources indicate that "We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Recent findings suggest that lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

How Sleep Helps the Brain Remove Waste.

Industry observers note that cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

According to recent reports, in 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

It has been revealed that building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

Industry observers note that "You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?".

How Pink Noise Amplifies Brain Waves.

In a recent development, to test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

Recent findings suggest that timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

Combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and promptly enough to synchronize the sound.

The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep.

The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

Sources indicate that the researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

It has been revealed that this possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a latest way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

Recent findings suggest that "Brain waste clearance is really key for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt claims.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has rolled out a tech giant that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

Industry observers note that for now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an important question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

According to recent reports, materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Anne Trafton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

It’s bringing new weekly challenges to the game, but its biggest addition is yet another Bonus Path to the battle pass. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

Similar to other Bonus Paths, the newly introduced Frostfire Bonus Path can be completed alongside the Season 1 battle pass. You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. It is worth noting, however, that Frostfire Points are only earned through weekly challenges, meaning there won’t be any bonus challenges associated with it.

Frostfire includes several newly introduced customisation rewards, of course, such as a Weapon Package, soldier skin, XP boosts and the usual run of unlocks.

Though the latest blog post may be devoid of any real details on Season 2, BF Studios confirmed that Battlefield Labs will play a larger role in offering a preview of what’s to come, so it’s entirely possible that the testing initiative will soon open its doors to players with an early look at some of the maps and other content planned for Season 2.

While we haven't gone into detail about most of the weapons here, we wanted to give you a quick overview of the best, the brightest, and, of course, most destructive tools in your arsenal to help you survive this perilous world.

Recent findings suggest that which weapons should you unlock in Dead Cells? It's a tough question, isn't it? You only have limited cells to spend on unlocking blueprints, so picking the best weapons to unlock can be tricky and overwhelming. We recommend starting with our S-tier weapons and working your way down from there. Most are ranked by their base damage numbers, but where a weapon or skill does something special and interesting, we've made sure to note it.

Of course, ultimately, it all comes down to personal preference. Make sure you read every weapon's description and decide if it would suit you. Some weapons have extra effects like applying a damage-over-time effect, like Bleed, or even combining with other weapons to create a one-two punch kind of effect. It's all personal. Dead Cells weapons tier list So, without further ado, let's get down to business. We've taken the time to break everything down by type for you: melee weapons, ranged weapons, shields (yes, they count), turrets and traps, and grenades. Each has its place in battle. Each will help you in some way to reach the end of the road.

If you disagree with anything on this list, then please let us know in the comments! These are a matter of opinion, after all, aside from their ranking on base damage. Critical damage is also important, so be sure to read the weapon description to take that into account.

Melee weapons make up the bread and butter of your arsenal, comprising everything from swords and axes to a spiked wrecking ball and a giant shark. Yes, a shark. Here, we've gone through and listed every melee weapon, ranked according to base damage.

Some weapons stand out more than others, of course. The Ferryman's Lantern allows you to kill an enemy to gather its soul. Then, as a secondary attack, charge it to fire those souls as projectiles, dealing critical hits if three souls are shot at the same time. With a base damage of 164 plus secondary damage of 107, then critical hits applying 429 damage, this is a monster of a weapon.

Sources indicate that others stand out for their usefulness and fun factor. With the Maw of the Deep, your third attack throws the shark, rooting the enemy and inflicting bleed. Rooted targets will then take critical damage - 158 base, and 270 critical.

The Rapier allows you to critical hit immediately after a roll or parry, and if you play the game like us, you'll be rolling around a lot anyway. With the Meat Skewer, your first attack places you behind the enemy, with your second hit applying critical damage. The Pure Nail comes courtesy of fellow Metroidvania Hollow Knight, allowing you to attack while moving left, right, and up. Drop down on an enemy and attack downwards to "bounce," just like in Hollow Knight, applying damage while in the air.

It has been revealed that finally, the Hard Light Sword is actually two weapons in one, along with the Hard Light Gun. A reference to the acclaimed Hyper Light Drifter, these weapons work in tandem. Fire the Hard Light Gun into enemies to damage and mark them. Then, the Hard Light Sword deals critical damage based on the number of shots it has received. Sword hits also recharge ammo for the gun, which (unlike other ranged weapons, more on those next) doesn't recharge over time. It's an elegant dance that might not be the most powerful, but is undoubtedly one of the most fun tools in the Dead Cells weapons arsenal.

According to recent reports, time for the first of our tier lists, then! Here we go: Rank Weapon S Ferryman's Lantern, Cursed Sword, War Spear, Tombstone, Flint, Oven Axe, Wrecking Ball, Giantkiller, Vampire Killer, Bible, Alucard's Sword, Death's Scythe, Misericorde A Toothpick, Symmetrical Lance, Shrapnel Axes, Hattori's Katana, Meat Skewer, Broadsword, Impaler, Crowbar, Twin Daggers, Hayabusa Boots, Vorpan, Shovel, Maw of the Deep, Rapier, Baseball Bat, Nutcracker, Pure Nail, Morning Star, Whip Sword, Sewing Scissors B Balanced Blade, Flashing Fans, Spite Sword, Rusty Sword, Bone, Swift Sword, Frantic Sword, Iron Staff, Assassin's Dagger, Rhythm n' Bouzouki, Seismic Strike, Wrenching Whip, Oiled Sword, Hayabusa Gauntlets, Blood Sword, Panchaku, Gold Digger, Machete and Pistol, Hard Light Sword, Giant Comb C Flawless, Sadist's Stiletto, Valmont's Whip, Torch, Abyssal Trident, Hand Hook, Spiked Boots, Bladed Tonfas, Dagger of Profit, Snake Fangs, Scythe Claw, Tentacle, King Scepter, Queen's Rapier, Starfury, Spartan Sandals.

It has been revealed that ranged weapons are extremely helpful in Dead Cells, especially when you don't want to get close to an enemy. Most use ammunition that regenerates over time, or can be retrieved from enemies on death or following a successful parry, in the case of arrows. Some, like the combined Hard Light Sword and Gun mentioned on the previous page, have a special function - in this case, ammo doesn't recharge passively and instead must be recharged by landing hits with the Hard Light Sword.

In a recent development, here's how we ranked the Dead Cells tier list for ranged weapons. Rank Weapon S Money Shooter, Ice Crossbow, Throwable Objects, Heavy Crossbow, Multiple-nocks Bow, Sonic Carbine, Barrel Launcher, Fire Blast, Magic Missiles, Medusa's Head, Anathema, Laser Glaive A Chakram of the Queen, The Boy's Axe, Peril Glyphs, Boomerang, Explosive Crossbow, Bow and Endless Quiver, Repeater Crossbow, Quick Bow, Laser Glaive, Gilded Yumi, Blowgun, Marksman's Bow, Ice Shards, Cross, Throwing Axe B Electric Whip, Lightning Bolt, War Javelin, Pyrotechnics, Nerves of Steel, Infantry Bow, Killing Deck, Hemorrhage C Beginner's Bow, Frost Blast, Ice Bow Firebrands, Hokuto's Bow, Magic Bow, Throwing Knife, Alchemic Carbine.

Shields might be a boring choice for your adventure through Dead Cells, but don't sleep on them. Hold down a shield's assigned button to hold it up after 0.37 seconds. Attacks that hit the front are reduced by the shield's damage absorption percentage, typically around 75%, while also dealing damage to the enemy by the damage number listed on the shield.

Shields can also be used to parry attacks. Tap the button rather than hold it down, and it attempts a parry. If no attack hits during that window, you can't block or parry again for a little under a second. If your parry is successful, then a few things can happen: you can parry or block again immediately and enjoy an additional effect, depending on the attack.

Carrying a shield also passively creates a force field for 0.5 seconds after you take damage, absorbing most damage except DoT effects like poison and some enemy attacks.

Sources indicate that here, we've ranked shields in Dead Cells by their base block damage, meaning the damage the enemy takes after you block an attack. As always, read the shield's in-game description for any interesting effects, like AoE damage. Rank Weapon S Spiked Shield, Greed Shield, Punishment, Knockback Shield, Alucard's Shield A Force Shield, Thunder Shield, Assault Shield, Front Line Shield, Ice Shield B Rampart, Bloodthirsty Shield C Old Wooden Shield, Cudgel, Parry Shield.

In a recent development, deployable skills in Dead Cells come in three forms: traps and turrets, grenades, and various miscellaneous powers. It isn't possible to start with these skills without the Recycling Tubes upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that first, let's cover deployable skills like traps and turrets. These come in powered and unpowered forms. Powered skills, such as turrets, need you to remain within their proximity for them to function. Line of sight is best, with the effective radius decreased if blocked by terrain. As long as you're within proximity, though, you'll notice a line of electricity connecting you to the deployed skill, allowing it to function.

Unpowered deployable skills are typically traps that don't actively attack on your behalf, such as traps that activate when the enemy steps onto them.

Let's rank the various types of deployable skills. First up, turrets. The Sinew Slicer is particularly worth noting. You'll come across it early, and it makes short work of early enemies without placing you in danger. Rank Skill S Barnacle, Scavenged Bombard, Heavy Turret, Cleaver A Double Crossb-o-matic, Sinew Slicer B Tesla Coil C Flamethrower Turret.

Next up, traps and miscellaneous powers. The Emergency Door skill simply spawns a door in front of you, which acts like a regular door, meaning it can be destroyed to stun enemies on the other side. The Night Light is extremely situational and can be deployed in the Forgotten Sepulcher to help with the Darkness. Requiring 120 seconds to recharge, it can be thrown to a location to create a temporary light at that location. Touch it to replenish your light aura. Rank Skill S Crusher A Explosive Decoy B Wolf Trap C Night Light, Emergency Door.

Grenades in Dead Cells do exactly what you expect: they explode. What more could you want? Simply throw, and enjoy! Some have added effects, of course, and can be paired with other skills or weapons for greater use. The Ice Grenade freezes enemies, for example, and the Root Grenade roots enemies, causing damage over time and keeping them rooted. The Magnetic Grenade is useful in crowded rooms. After a few moments, it attracts enemies in a large area, then explodes to deal electrical damage over time.

Grenades, like other skills, aren't exactly consumables as you would expect in other games. Rather they each have a set cooldown, meaning they can be reused over and over again.

Recent findings suggest that the Hunter's Grenade is situational, which is why it's ranked C, but it's quite useful at the same time. Throw it to "annoy" a monster. When its health drops to 40% or less, use "Blueprint Extractor" to grab a blueprint. Rank Skill S Powerful Grenade, Holy Water A Infantry Grenade, Cluster Grenade, Magnetic Grenade B Stun Grenade, Ice Grenade, Fire Grenade, Root Grenade, Oil Grenade, Swarm C Hunter's Grenade.

#52022. Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought

Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected.
  • According to recent reports, in a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root.
  • "Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," mentioned study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected. Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) have now uncovered a surprising pattern: Certain regions of the heart appear to be hotspots for aging-related inflammation, offering new clues about how the heart changes over time.

According to recent reports, in a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root. These areas contain immune cells and connective tissue cells whose interactions change with age, potentially affecting the surrounding heart muscle. The findings provide a new picture of cardiac aging and could guide future efforts to understand cardiovascular disease.

"Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," mentioned study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. "We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don't age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don't age at the same rate either, even within one individual.".

According to recent reports, much of the previous research on heart aging has centered on cardiac muscle, particularly the left ventricle. This chamber performs the essential task of pumping blood into the aorta and throughout the body. By studying the heart as a whole, rather than concentrating primarily on its muscle, the JAX team uncovered important changes in other tissues and the ways their cells interact.

"The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine," Rosenthal said. "It turns out they're home to many of the cells we're interested in, and that's where some of the most notable aging-related signals were concentrated.".

Mapping Hidden Hotspots of Heart Aging.

Recent findings suggest that growing older is the single greatest risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet many of the cellular processes responsible for the heart's decline remain poorly understood. One challenge is that mammalian heart muscle cells have very little ability to regenerate or replace themselves. To investigate what happens as the heart ages, Rosenthal and her colleagues used advanced techniques that allowed them to study thousands of individual cells from young and old mice while also identifying their locations within the heart.

Scientists already know that aging is accompanied by a persistent, low level of inflammation throughout the body. Earlier studies have found similar changes in the heart, including an increase in immune cells that regulate inflammatory activity (macrophages) and cells that produce and maintain connective tissue and contribute to scar formation (fibroblasts).

Recent findings suggest that the new analysis showed that aging macrophages became more active in genes involved in inflammation and changes to tissue structure. Fibroblasts, meanwhile, increasingly displayed molecular characteristics associated with fibrosis (or scarring). Crucially, the researchers went beyond identifying which genes were active. They also mapped the locations of these cells, making it possible to see how different regions of the heart change as they grow older.

This approach revealed that inflammation and fibrosis (or scarring) were not distributed uniformly. Instead, the strongest signals appeared around the heart valves and aortic root. The researchers believe these regions may act as vital centers of cardiac aging, where changes in supporting cells could influence the health of nearby heart muscle.

"To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life," Rosenthal mentioned. "What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging.".

Surprising Signs of Aging in Young Hearts.

It has been revealed that another unexpected discovery challenged assumptions about how scientists identify aging cells. The team examined molecular markers frequently associated with cellular senescence, a state in which cells permanently lose the ability to divide, often because of aging or stress. As senescent cells accumulate, they can contribute to ongoing inflammation, tissue damage, and diseases associated with older age.

In a recent development, surprisingly, some of these supposedly age-related markers were already present in young mouse hearts. Their presence suggests that the markers alone cannot reliably establish whether a cell has entered senescence, and that their meaning may depend on where they appear and the condition of the surrounding tissue.

According to recent reports, "What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren't where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us," Rosenthal mentioned. "That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don't mean a cell is senescent. There's nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart.".

The researchers also identified genes that became more active with age and were especially prominent in the same regions. Among them were Ccl8, which helps transmit inflammatory signals, and Cdkn1a (also known as p21), a gene widely used as an indicator of cellular senescence. Their locations provided further evidence that the valves and aortic root may be particularly important areas for understanding how the heart ages.

"We're not talking about single genes. We're talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts," Rosenthal noted.

Male and Female Hearts Show Different Aging Patterns.

The study uncovered another important distinction: Aging did not produce exactly the same molecular changes in male and female mouse hearts.

In males, aging fibroblasts indicated stronger connections to biological processes associated with fibrosis. In females, the corresponding changes were more closely related to pathways involved in heart development and protein production.

Rosenthal noted that these differences may offer clues about cardiovascular aging in humans. Heart disease tends to become more common in women after menopause, while its development in men generally follows a more gradual pattern. The distinct cellular changes observed in male and female mice could help researchers investigate the biological processes behind these differences.

Sources indicate that however, the results describe differences in molecular activity, not demonstrated differences in heart function or disease risk. Further research will be needed to determine how these patterns influence cardiovascular health.

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the team compared the mouse results with previously published data from human hearts. Several molecular processes associated with aging, including pathways involved in responding to cellular stress, appeared in both species. This overlap suggests that at least some of the biological changes identified in mice may also be relevant to human heart aging.

"Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process," stated study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.

Could These Discoveries Help Protect Aging Hearts?

It has been revealed that although the research does not yet identify a new treatment, it offers scientists a more detailed understanding of where aging-related changes occur and which cells are involved. By revealing these cellular patterns, the findings could help guide future studies aimed at reducing cardiovascular decline, maintaining healthy heart function, and improving health later in life.

Rosenthal's team is now examining whether exercise, diet, and disease alter the interactions between immune cells and connective tissue cells. The researchers hope to distinguish the normal effects of aging from changes that may leave the heart increasingly vulnerable to cardiovascular problems.

The experimental design also helped the team isolate aging itself as a contributing factor. Because the mice lived under the same conditions and received the same diet, the researchers could investigate age-related changes without the additional variation introduced by different environments or eating habits.

According to recent reports, "Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the substantial questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself," noted study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. "Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta.".

Together, the findings suggest that understanding heart aging requires looking beyond the muscle responsible for pumping blood. The valves, major blood vessels, and supporting cells may play a much larger role than previously recognized. Learning how these structures change and communicate over time could eventually help scientists identify ways to preserve cardiovascular health as people age.

Research Funding and Study Authors.

The research received funding from the NIH Common Fund through The Jackson Laboratory Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (JAX-Sen TMC U54 AG079753). Additional support came from JAX's National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center (P30 CA034196).

Additional authors from The Jackson Laboratory included Yue Zhao, Antonios Somarakis, Harshpreet Chandok, Juliana Alcoforado Diniz, Ramalakshmi Ramasamy, Gretchen T. Clark, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, and J. Matthew Mahoney. Leon Frommer and Sikander Hayat of RWTH Aachen University also contributed to the study.

Sources indicate that materials provided by Jackson Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Latest Update: Petit Planet Hands-On Preview – Creature Comforts

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia.
  • The game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z).
  • In a recent development, story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia. The creators of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero have crafted well-received, lucrative free-to-play gacha games across several disparate genres; Petit Planet, fittingly, sees it try to attract yet another world of players. It’s been a year since I first played Petit Planet’s initial alpha test, and I spent a couple of more hours exploring its cozy cosmos at the Hoyoverse Media Tour in Seoul, South Korea. Although what I played has not dramatically changed my opinion of the game – it remains a delightful, if familiar, good time – speaking to its lead designer who goes by the single name Murphy and lead artist Yunli Huang helped shed light on how Petit Planet will differentiate itself from contemporaries and its approach to multiplayer, storytelling, and monetization.

The game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z). Although you are ostensibly human, everyone else is a talking animal. Your mentor of sorts is a chillax sheepdog named Mobai, who enjoys wearing straw hats and dropping his catchphrase/life mantra “Mo worries” and “Mo Rush.” The business-minded Glenn the Squirrel is a shopkeeper and seems like a cuter, less aggressive Tom Nook. Yunghou is a shy fox who enjoys farming and has the slightest hint of a southern accent. These critters and many more inhabit your planet, which you’ll grow from an empty (but vibrant) rock into a bustling village filled with homes, businesses, crops, decor, and, of course, neighbors.

In a recent development, story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer. Still, after Pokémon Pokopia presented an unexpectedly wild and fascinating tale, I ask if players should bother getting invested in a grander narrative à la Genshin Impact. The short answer seems to be “not so much.”.

Sources indicate that “Unlike other Hoyoverse games, there is no such main plot,” Murphy explains in my group interview. “There will be a main story at the beginning, but the main purpose is just to guide the players, get more familiar with the setting and the world. But the whole narrative of this game will be more fragmented. For example, if you look at those descriptions of those items, there will be a lot of content and narrative behind it. If you look at the description of creatures, many of them are real creatures in real world, and you get to learn more knowledge of this creature by reading those descriptions. And also, we've developed a very comprehensive narrative for each of our neighbors, so that is also part of our, called like, main plot, main narrative, because we want to make this world more like more lively and a more livable world. So that is how we treat narrative in this game.".

In a recent development, while players who enjoy a substantial story to propel them through a game may be disappointed, those looking to unwind with a laid-back experience should be pleased. Hoyoverse is designing Petit Planet to be a no-pressure experience to enjoy at your leisure, hence why it emphasizes it as a life sim more than a management sim. There are no complicated stats to manage; simple inputs make it easy to pick up and play; imperfection is encouraged, with Hoyoverse comparing the experience to doodling as a child: your creation may not be perfect, but you had fun bringing your imagination to life.

Recent findings suggest that I spent the first hour of my roughly two-and-a-half-hour session starting from scratch to see if any notable changes were made to this introductory portion in the last year. If there are any differences, they’re imperceptible because I wen went through the same onboarding of learning how to catch bugs and fish, building your first home, inviting your first neighbor, and farming crops, all while growing a magical sapling that, after performing enough tasks, blooms into a full tree that brings new life and mechanics to your world as it grows. Performing special tasks for residents, from completing requests to simply interacting with them, grows their bond, which, when high enough, will entice them to move in. For veteran genre fans, it’s a familiar song and dance. What I did notice this time around is how refreshingly quick the onboarding is. You have all of these foundational mechanics within the first 45 to 50 minutes, which is a nice pace. It was a good refresher for some foundational mechanics I’d forgotten since I last played, but it created an appetite to dive deeper.

Sources indicate that thankfully, Hoyoverse provided a second build set many hours into the game to give an idea of how planets can evolve. This build was set during winter, one of Petit Planet’s revolving seasons that alter the environment and introduce themed cosmetics and decor for players and residents. Sporting winter gear, I ran around the snow-covered planet, which was densely populated with shops, homes, and neighbors. I was initially greeted by unfamiliar faces named Trixie and Kookoo, who provided weather forecasts and news reports reminiscent of Isabelle from Animal Crossing and Callie and Marie from Splatoon. My sparse quest log was tricky to tackle since they revolved around mechanics I had no context for, such as setting up Vignettes. These are essentially templates for unique scenes filled out by dropping the correct furniture pieces in their layout; in this case, I had to set up an outdoor movie on the beach.

I only spent roughly an hour with this late build, and my biggest takeaway was simply how dense and lovely the village looked. A lot of work went into crafting this build, which boasted a farm filled with different crops (with unlockable recipes to create dishes from them), crafting tables to build furniture from collectible blueprints, and several shops, including Glenn’s to purchase a revolving selection of decor items. None of what I saw surprised me, however. Petit Planet so far checks many of the boxes you’d expect and want from a life sim. My cursory tour of a later-game planet did little to reveal any big new ideas, but what I did experience seemed perfectly cromulent.

According to recent reports, my biggest question regards multiplayer. As much as I enjoy Animal Crossing: New Horizons and Pokémon Pokopia as solo experiences, playing with friends feels like a mean joke because of the tedious number of hoops to jump through just to invite other players into your world. And even once your buddy arrives, interactions are disappointingly limited. When I ask if Petit Planet offers a comparatively frictionless multiplayer experience, Murphy vaguely assures smoother sailing. “The multiplayer experience is a very important part of our game because, just as the interaction with NPCs, the interaction with other players is also a form of building up emotional connection to this game, and we want to provide that kind of experience to our players.” More specifically, Murphy cites features such as dynamic server load adjustments based on player counts and the option to allow or ban visiting players from taking resources from your planet to prevent griefing.

As a free-to-play Hoyoverse game, monetization is a major talking point. In Petit Planet’s case, the team agrees that rolling for neighbors gacha-style would be strange and defeats the spirit of the genre. Instead, all monetization will revolve around cosmetics; players can unlock new furniture and themed decor sets, outfits, and other cosmetic accessories for their character. Unlocking a full themed set of decor earns currency points, and there are myriad reward meters to fill for performing mundane tasks like greeting residents or catching bugs. It remains to be seen if and how Petit Planet’s progression begins nudging players into opening their wallets, but Hoyoverse promises it will be an experience that deemphasizes grinding.

I also briefly checked out the recently unveiled Switch 2 version of Petit Planet. My impressions after about 15 minutes of playtime: it’s fine. It sometimes ran noticeably hitchier than the PC version I spent most of my time with, but it seems perfectly adequate so far and, hopefully, will be a smooth experience when it launches sometime next year.

According to recent reports, since life sims require more than a couple of hours to fully reveal their quality, it was tough to get a read on Petit Planet even with this new showing. The game looks beautiful thanks to Hoyoverse’s signature sharp and colorful visual style. It has a relaxing vibe, and feels mechanically decent for the most part. In short, it seems broadly fine and like a respectable take on the genre. I suspect its biggest appeal will be that it will receive what Animal Crossing: New Horizons lacked: years of constant, substantial support.

Hoyoverse is very good about keeping fans of its games well fed with regular updates for years on end, and I don’t expect it to stop now. The idea of a seemingly well-made spin on Animal Crossing that’s free to download and, unless it completely bombs, will almost certainly receive years of new content is enticing on paper. I imagine this is the reason Petit Planet is coming to Switch 2 next year, where it can lure in Animal Crossing and Pokopia players before other consoles. PC and mobile players, meanwhile, must only wait until December 4 when Petit Planet fully launches to see if it has the chops to stand alongside the coziest giants of the genre.

Latest Update: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open upcoming possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders.
  • Sources indicate that the findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins.
  • Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open upcoming possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

Sources indicate that the findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms.

In a recent development, the discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

Industry observers note that worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling notable features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

Industry observers note that "We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12.".

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Recent findings suggest that although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

Sources indicate that "Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide upcoming insights into human diseases," indicates Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a fresh world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a fresh Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

According to recent reports, at the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the fresh 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

It has been revealed that then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the latest regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Recent findings suggest that of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

Sources indicate that in November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free enhancement, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#52013. Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • It has been revealed that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • Industry observers note that quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

It has been revealed that the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Industry observers note that quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A Upcoming Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

According to recent reports, quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

In a recent development, but quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

Sources indicate that rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the latest approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify notable interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

According to recent reports, "From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

In a recent development, after this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, highlighted that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

According to recent reports, the next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

Industry observers note that "After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," states Peter Zoller.

This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that since time immemorial, North American and European publishers have racked their brains over ways to make their games sell in Japan, ancient heartland of mythical beings like Mario, Sonic, and Polaroid Pete.
  • Industry observers note that speaking to me last week, Rockstar North's former technical director Obbe Vermeij shared a little about the abandoned project.
  • It has been revealed that rockstar's parent company Take-Two Interactive filed a trademark for GTA Tokyo back in 2003, the year before the release of the Los Angeles-flavoured GTA: San Andreas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that since time immemorial, North American and European publishers have racked their brains over ways to make their games sell in Japan, ancient heartland of mythical beings like Mario, Sonic, and Polaroid Pete. In the late noughties, Microsoft launched a major push to give Japanese youth the Xbox virus with such targeted console exclusives as Blue Dragon and Lost Odyssey. And Rockstar once dreamed of making a Grand Theft Auto game set in Tokyo.

Industry observers note that speaking to me last week, Rockstar North's former technical director Obbe Vermeij shared a little about the abandoned project. Emphasis on the "little" – it doesn't appear to have gotten very far, despite recently unearthed allusions to "Tokyo PS2" in GTA 5's source code.

It has been revealed that rockstar's parent company Take-Two Interactive filed a trademark for GTA Tokyo back in 2003, the year before the release of the Los Angeles-flavoured GTA: San Andreas. At the time, Rockstar were apparently looking at collaborating with a Japanese studio on the project. "So this was kind above my pay grade," Vermeij told me. "But yeah, there were negotiations with studios, and I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it, because then it becomes like a bigger thing than it is, and I'll probably get it wrong, and I don't know how far the negotiations were, how serious it was. I mean, it was definitely serious. It was the plan. But I don't know how close it got to actually happening.".

The game itself would likely have been a contemporary story, not a historical yarn like Rockstar's subsequent Red Dead Redemption. "It definitely had samurai swords in it, I remember that, but I think it was present-day probably," Vermeij went on. "Or sort of not too [far off] - it wasn't, like, sort of the medieval era in Japanese history, or anything. It was definitely not like that.".

Vermeij was at Rockstar from 1995 to 2009, where he worked on the first four mainline 3D GTA games, plus some handheld spin-offs. During that time, he says, Rockstar frequently considered the idea of a Grand Theft Auto set outside the United States. "In the same way that we were always thinking about other games, we also thought about cities that would be cool, and it was always the same list," he noted. "It was Moscow, London. Istanbul, Rio de Janeiro, maybe Paris and Tokyo. It was always the same ones that people suggested.".

According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto has never quite the money-spinner in Japan that it is in North America and Europe. Localised editions of the original three 3D GTA games were published by Capcom, sometime after the original releases, selling a few hundred thousand copies apiece in their launch years.

"I think perhaps [Rockstar's co-founders] the Housers were a little annoyed that GTA wasn't as substantial in Japan as they thought it deserved to be," Vermeij reflected. "So it kind of made sense to get a local studio to do it. Japanese people actually kind of like different games from westerners a fair bit. For instance, they don't like first person shooters and stuff. So, it made sense to have a Japanese studio have a shot at it, and I think it would have been really cool, because you know, a GTA made by somebody else in Japanese culture – that's something I would probably play.".

Take-Two ultimately abandoned their original "GTA Tokyo" trademark in 2008. It's not clear how much Rockstar have considered setting GTA overseas since Vermeij's day, but co-founder Dan Houser (who left the manufacturer in 2020) recently told podcaster Lex Fridman that they ultimately decided it wasn't a credible objective.

“We made a little thing in London 26 years ago - GTA London - for the top-down for PS1," he said. "That was pretty cute and fun, as the first mission pack ever for PlayStation 1. I think for a full GTA game, we always decided there was so much Americana inherent in the IP, it would be really hard to make it work in London or anywhere else. You know, you needed guns, you needed these larger-than-life characters. It just felt like the game was so much about America, possibly from an outsider's perspective. But that was so much about what the thing was that it wouldn't really have worked in the same way elsewhere.”.

In a recent development, if this article has left you pining for the Shibuya Scramble NPC-tipping sim that will never be, I bring good news: Japanese developers are quite capable of making their own urban open worlders. The obvious go-tos are Sega's Yakuza/Like A Dragon games, with their abundance of lovingly modelled eateries and discount stores. There's also Ghostwire: Tokyo, a respectable first-person parkour sim, though this particular incarnation of Tokyo has a lot of paranormal congestion. All these games have the advantage of being playable on PC right now. As for GTA 6? Who can say, but Vermeij thinks Rockstar might want to port it sooner to get ahead of the slopcomp craze.

The game also comes with a wide range of modern technologies, including Nvidia DLSS Super Resolution, and Frame Generation. Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are supported, too.
